another.title: What a syllogism is and its parts
paragraphs: Here is another way to see it. Think of a syllogism as a short chain of three links, where the first two are things you are simply handed and the third is the thing you are asked to accept. Say I tell you that all poodles are dogs, and that all dogs are mammals. Those two statements are the premises, the starting points. Then I say, so all poodles are mammals. That last sentence is the conclusion, the place the reasoning lands.

Why does the landing hold? Imagine nesting boxes. The poodles fit in a box labeled dogs, and the dogs box fits inside a bigger box labeled mammals. If one box sits inside a second, and the second sits inside a third, then the first is automatically inside the third. You never had to inspect a single poodle. The conclusion follows purely from how the boxes sit inside each other, and that is what deductive means: if the premises are true, the conclusion has no choice.

So if a friend asks what a syllogism is, you can say it is two given statements about categories, using words like all, no or some, plus a third statement that either has to follow from them or does not. Your whole job is to sort the three statements and ask whether the last one is forced. That is different from the if-then kind, which starts from a condition instead of from categories.

another.title: How to check validity, step by step
paragraphs: Here is another way to see it. Suppose I tell you that all of my cats are hungry, and that some hungry animals are noisy, and then I conclude that some of my cats are noisy. It sounds fine. So do what a careful person does and try to build a scene where both premises are true and the conclusion is false. Put three animals in my kitchen, two cats and a dog, all hungry, and let the dog be the only noisy one. All my cats are hungry, yes. Some hungry animals are noisy, yes, the dog. But no cat is noisy.

That one scene is the whole proof that the conclusion does not have to follow, because the word some never said which hungry animals make the noise. Now change the second premise to all hungry animals are noisy, and try to break the conclusion that all my cats are noisy. Every cat is hungry and every hungry animal is noisy, so there is no scene that keeps the premises and escapes the conclusion. That is what valid feels like: you hunt hard and every attempt fails.

So when you explain it aloud, say that you picture a situation, guess a conclusion, and then try to wreck the guess by building a different situation that still fits the premises. One scene that wrecks it is enough to call it not valid. Only if every scene you can build keeps the conclusion standing is it valid.

another.title: Validity versus truth
paragraphs: Here is another way to see it. Think of validity as how well a machine is built, and truth as what you happen to feed into it. Imagine a machine designed so that when you give it all X are Y and all Y are Z, it hands back all X are Z. That machine works every time, whatever you put in. Now feed it silly things: all the pets in my house are robots, and all robots run on batteries. Out comes, all the pets in my house run on batteries. The machine did its job, so the reasoning is valid, but the conclusion is false, because my pets are not robots. The bad input is to blame, not the machine.

Feed the same machine true things: all poodles are dogs, and all dogs are mammals, so all poodles are mammals. Same machine, true inputs, true output. That is the promise of validity: a good machine plus true premises gives a true conclusion, and nothing beyond that.

Now picture a badly built machine. All dogs are animals, and some animals are pets, so some dogs are pets. Every sentence there happens to be true, even the conclusion, and still the reasoning is not valid, because you can picture a world where the only pets are hamsters. The premises would still hold and the conclusion would fail. A true ending does not rescue weak reasoning. Tell your friend that validity asks whether the conclusion has to follow, truth asks whether it matches the world, and you answer those two questions separately.

another.title: Belief bias
paragraphs: Here is another way to see it. Imagine a friend reads you this: all of the cafe's pastries are sweet, and some sweet things are bad for your teeth, so some of the cafe's pastries are bad for your teeth. You nod before they finish, because you already believe sugary pastries are rough on teeth. That quick nod is belief bias at work. The ending matched what you think, so the argument got waved through.

Slow it down and test the reasoning instead of the ending. Picture the pastries as sweet but gentle, say soft fruit tarts. Picture some hard candy elsewhere in the world that is sweet and bad for teeth. Both premises are true in that picture, and not one pastry from the cafe is bad for teeth. So the conclusion was never forced, even though it might well be true in real life. The premises just did not earn it.

A handy question to ask yourself is what you would do if the ending were something you did not believe, with the very same shape. If you would hunt for an exception then, hunt for one now. The pull you feel toward a believable ending is a feeling about the world, while validity is about whether the conclusion follows. Pull those apart and you stop being fooled. Sounding right is not the same as following.

another.title: Conditional syllogisms: the four forms cheat sheet
paragraphs: Here is another way to see it, using a rule everyone trusts: if it rains, the ground is wet. Here p is it rains and q is the ground is wet. Say it rains. Then the ground is wet, no question, and that is the forward direction. Say the ground is dry. Then it cannot have rained, because rain would have left it wet, so that is the backward direction, and it works too. Those are the two valid forms.

Now try the other two. Say the ground is wet. Did it rain? Not necessarily, because a sprinkler or a spilled bucket would do the same. The rule said what rain brings about, not that rain is the only cause. And say it did not rain. Is the ground dry? Not necessarily, for the very same sprinkler reason. Both wrong forms fail because they treat the rule as if it also said that rain is the only way to a wet ground.

So when you explain it aloud, hang on to rain and wet ground. Rain happened, so wet. Not wet, so no rain. Those are safe. Wet, so rain? Not safe. No rain, so not wet? Not safe. The valid ones begin with p being true or with q being false, and the invalid ones begin with q being true or p being false.

another.title: Modus ponens and modus tollens (the valid ones)
paragraphs: Here is another way to see it. Think about a rule at a concert gate: if you have a ticket, you are let in. Modus ponens is the easy one. The guard sees you holding a ticket, so you go in. You start at the condition and walk forward along the arrow, and nobody finds that confusing.

Modus tollens is the same rule read from the far end. Suppose the guard tells you that a certain person was not let in. What do you know about their ticket? They did not have one, because a ticket would have gotten them through. Notice that you reasoned without ever seeing their pockets. You only needed the rule and the fact that the promised result did not happen. A board game gives the same shape: if you roll a six, you move again. Your friend did not move again, so they did not roll a six.

This feels harder only because you travel against the arrow, from a result that did not happen back to a condition that did not happen. The logic is just as solid as going forward. When you tell a friend, say that if the promised result is missing, the condition cannot have been there, because if it had been there, the result would have followed.

another.title: Why syllogisms 3 and 4 are not valid
paragraphs: Here is another way to see it. Take a rule so plain that nobody can argue with it: if it is a golden retriever, then it is a dog. Now try the two shaky moves. It is a dog, so it is a golden retriever? Clearly not, it could be a beagle. It is not a golden retriever, so it is not a dog? Again clearly not, because that same beagle is not a golden retriever and is still a dog. These feel silly here, but they are exactly the two invalid forms, with content that makes the flaw impossible to miss.

Why do they fail? The rule only says where golden retrievers end up, which is inside the dog group. It says nothing about the dog group containing only golden retrievers, and nothing about animals outside the retriever group. When a conclusion feels right in another case, it is usually because you quietly added the word only to the rule. Try a cafe: if you show a student card, you get a discount. Someone got a discount, so they showed a card? Maybe they had a coupon. Someone showed no card, so they got no discount? Maybe they had the coupon.

So when a form feels shaky, put in something like retrievers and dogs, where you already know the answer, and see whether the same shape gives nonsense. If it does, the shape is invalid wherever it shows up. The first premise supports going forward from the condition and backward from a missing result, and nothing else.

another.title: Mental models (Johnson-Laird, 1999) and the pool table
paragraphs: Here is another way to see it. Imagine three pets on a shelf. I tell you the cat is to the left of the dog, and the fish tank is to the right of the dog. Where is the cat compared with the tank? You do not need a rule. You picture cat, dog, tank in a row, and the cat is plainly to the left of the tank. That little picture is a mental model, one concrete way the statements could be true, the same kind of picture you hold when you work out the pool table.

Now make it trickier. The hamster is to the left of the dog, and the fish tank is also to the left of the dog. Is the hamster to the left of the tank? Picture hamster, tank, dog, and it seems so. But a careful person tries another arrangement that fits the same statements: tank, hamster, dog. Both statements are still true, and now the hamster is to the right of the tank. That single picture falsifies the tentative conclusion, because the statements never decided the order. In the first shelf puzzle every arrangement you can build gives the same answer, which is why that one holds up.

That is the whole method in plain words. Picture a situation, guess what follows, then try to build a different picture that still fits but breaks your guess. One picture that breaks it is enough. And just as with the pool table, you are not applying a formula, you are using the ability you already have to picture where things are.

another.title: The Wason four-card problem (abstract)
paragraphs: Here is another way to see it. Suppose someone hands you four cards and says: if a card has a circle on one side, then the other side is blue. You can see a circle, a square, a blue card and a green card. Which ones could prove the rule wrong? Forget which cards agree with the rule, and ask of each one whether its hidden side could embarrass the rule.

The circle could, because if the back is any color other than blue, the rule is broken, so you turn it. The green card could too, because if a circle is hiding on its back, that is a circle with a non-blue side, exactly what the rule forbids, so you turn it. The square tells you nothing, since the rule only speaks about circles. And the blue card cannot hurt the rule either: a circle behind it is fine, and a square behind it is fine, because the rule never said only circles may sit behind blue. So you turn the circle and the green card.

The blue card is the tempting one, because finding a circle there would feel like a win. But a win that could never have been a loss proves nothing. When you explain it aloud, say that to test an if-then rule you hunt for the case that would break it, which is a circle with no blue, and you check only the cards that could be hiding that case: the circle itself, and the card that is not blue.

another.title: Concrete Wason version and permission schemas
paragraphs: Here is another way to see it. Picture a library with this rule: if someone is borrowing a book to take home, then they must have a library card. Four people stand at the desk, and you can only see one side of each. One is carrying a book out the door. One is just reading at a table. One shows a library card. One has no card. Who do you need to check?

You probably answered without effort. Check the person leaving with a book, to see whether they have a card. Check the person with no card, to see whether they are taking a book. The reader at the table breaks nothing, because the rule never limited reading. The person with a card breaks nothing either, because a card holder is allowed to borrow or not borrow. Nobody had to explain falsification to you. You just knew this is a permission rule, a condition that must be met before an action is allowed, so the cheating to look for is the action without the permission.

Notice that this has the same shape as the vowel and even number puzzle, so the logic did not change. What changed is that the rule matched a familiar pattern, the permission schema, and it told you what to check. The beer and 21 rule works the same way. Keep the caution in mind, though: it is not familiarity alone that helps, it is a setting that calls up the idea of permission.

another.title: Framing effect: gain versus loss
paragraphs: Here is another way to see it. Suppose a pizza party has ten slices that might get ruined by a leaky oven, and you must pick a plan. Put it as saving. Plan one: five slices will be saved for certain. Plan two: a half chance that all ten are saved and a half chance that none are. Put it as losing. Plan three: five slices will be ruined for certain. Plan four: a half chance that none are ruined and a half chance that all ten are ruined.

Now look under the words. Five saved for certain means five ruined, so plans one and three are the same plan. A half chance of saving all ten is a half chance of ruining none, so plans two and four are the same gamble. Four plans, only two real options. The framing effect says people lean toward the sure option when the choices talk about gains and toward the gamble when they talk about losses, even though nothing about the slices has changed.

Why would wording do that? Saved points your attention at what you keep, and a sure thing feels good. Ruined points your attention at what you lose, and a sure loss feels worse than a chance of dodging it, so the gamble looks more attractive. This pizza case is only my own illustration of the pattern, not a result from anyone. What you can say aloud is that the facts stayed the same, the words changed, and the choice changed with them, so the switch comes from the wording and not from the outcomes.
